title: Economics in History and Geography: Industry, Labor, Trade, Maps, and Migration
objectives: You will explain how industrialization changed work, cities, and the U.S. economy, and trace cause-and-effect chains in economic history.
You will describe why workers formed labor unions and how government responded to labor problems.
You will use opportunity cost and comparative advantage to explain specialization and trade, and predict the effects of tariffs, quotas, and embargoes.
You will locate places using latitude and longitude and identify hemispheres and directions on a map grid.
You will apply the themes of geography, including regions, human-environment interaction, and push and pull factors in migration.

slides.title: Economics in History and Geography
slides.board:
Week 8 Social Studies: Industry, Labor, Trade, Maps, and Migration

Today you will:

  • Trace how industrialization changed work and cities
  • Explain why workers organized and how government responded
  • Use opportunity cost and comparative advantage to explain trade, and predict the effects of tariffs
  • Locate places with latitude and longitude
  • Apply the themes of geography, human-environment interaction, and push and pull factors

Plan: Warm-up → four big ideas → we do it together → you do it → GED questions

notes.say: Last week we learned the tools of economics: scarcity, opportunity cost, supply and demand, money, and policy. This week we use those tools on real history and on maps. Economics and geography together are about 30 percent of the GED Social Studies test, and many history questions are really economics questions in disguise: why did people move, why did prices change, why did workers strike? Today we answer four kinds of questions: what caused a change, who gains and who loses from trade, where a place is, and why people move.
ask: Think of someone in your family who moved to a new town or took a factory, warehouse, or farm job. What made them move or change jobs? (Expected: any honest answer. Write it down; we will label it later as a push or pull factor.)
notes.watch: Some students feel geography is "just memorizing." Tell them up front: the GED never asks for a capital city from memory. It gives a map, grid, or table and asks them to read it.

slides.title: Warm-up: Week 7 Economics Review
slides.board:
Answer each one.

  1. A cafe raises the price of muffins from $2 to $3. By the law of demand, what happens to the quantity of muffins people buy?
  2. At $4 a ticket, fans want 300 tickets; the team offers 500. Shortage or surplus? How large?
  3. Tara ranks her Saturday choices: (1) work a paid shift, (2) go to the beach, (3) clean the garage. She works. What is her opportunity cost?
  4. The Federal Reserve raises interest rates to fight inflation. Is this fiscal or monetary policy?
steps: 1. Quantity demanded falls. When the price goes up, people buy less.
2. A surplus of 200 tickets: 500 offered − 300 wanted = 200 left unsold. The price is above equilibrium.
3. The beach trip: only the next-best choice she gave up, not the beach and the garage together.
4. Monetary policy: the Federal Reserve controls interest rates and the money supply. Fiscal policy is taxes and spending by Congress and the President.

notes.say: These four questions review last week. Give the student about three minutes, then have them say each answer before you reveal it. Opportunity cost matters most today, because comparative advantage is built on it. If question 3 is shaky, spend an extra minute: opportunity cost is the single next-best thing you give up.
ask: In question 2, what would happen to the price if the team could change it? (Expected: it would fall toward equilibrium so more tickets sell)
notes.answer: 1. Quantity demanded falls. 2. Surplus of 200 tickets. 3. The beach trip (next-best choice only). 4. Monetary policy.
notes.watch: On question 3, students often say "the beach and cleaning the garage." Opportunity cost is only the next-best alternative, because she could not have done both anyway.

slides.title: Industrialization: From Hand to Machine
slides.board:
Industrialization = the shift from making goods by hand to making them with machines in factories.

WhenWhat happened
about 1790First successful water-powered cotton mill in the U.S. (Pawtucket, Rhode Island)
1820s–1830sLowell, Massachusetts, textile mills hire young women from farms
1825Erie Canal links the Great Lakes to New York City
1869Transcontinental railroad completed
late 1800sGiant steel (Carnegie) and oil (Rockefeller) companies; Sherman Antitrust Act, 1890

Effects: cheaper goods · factory jobs · people move to cities

notes.say: Industrialization began in Great Britain in the late 1700s and reached the United States around 1790, when Samuel Slater, a British-trained mechanic, helped start a water-powered cotton-spinning mill in Rhode Island. Factories could make cloth, shoes, and later steel far more cheaply than skilled workers could by hand. Transportation was the second engine: the Erie Canal in 1825 and the transcontinental railroad in 1869 let factories sell to the whole country. The big effect for the GED is the chain: factories need workers, so people leave farms for cities. In 1860 about one American in five lived in an urban area; the 1920 census was the first to count more than half.
ask: Why would a canal or railroad help a factory owner? (Expected: cheaper, faster shipping lets the factory sell to more customers far away)
What is one effect of industrialization on where people lived? (Expected: they moved from farms to cities)
notes.watch: Students sometimes think "industrialization" means only big companies. Keep the definition simple: machines and factories replacing handwork.

slides.title: Worked Example: Reading the Urban Graph
slides.board:
The graph shows the percent of Americans living in urban areas (places with 2,500 or more people), by census year.

(a) In which census year shown did more than half of Americans first live in urban areas?
(b) By how many percentage points did the urban share rise from 1880 to 1920?

figure.title: Percent of U.S. Population Living in Urban Areas

steps: Read the title, labels, and units. The y-axis is a percent of the whole population, so "half" means 50%.
(a) Values: 19.8, 25.7, 28.2, 35.1, 39.6, 45.6, 51.2. The first value above 50 is 51.2 in 1920.
(b) 1920 value − 1880 value = 51.2 − 28.2 = 23.0 percentage points.
Connect to history: the line rises in every decade shown, the same years factories and railroads grew. The graph shows when cities grew; the history explains why.

notes.say: Model the data routine out loud: title, labels, units, then the exact numbers. Write each value on the board before you calculate. Point out that subtracting two percentages gives percentage points, not percent. This graph uses real census data, and the GED loves this kind of graph paired with a question about causes.
ask: Did the urban share ever fall between two census years on this graph? (Expected: No, it rose every decade)
Between which two census years was the rise largest? (Expected: 1880 to 1890, 6.9 points)
notes.watch: For (b), some students subtract from the wrong year or write "23%." Have them circle both years in the question before reading the graph, and say "points" when they subtract.

slides.title: Labor: Problems and Responses
slides.board:
Problem in factoriesWorkers respondedGovernment responded
10–12 hour days, 6 days a weekLabor unions (AFL, 1886)1935 Wagner Act: right to organize and bargain
Low pay; one worker has no powerCollective bargaining1938 Fair Labor Standards Act: minimum wage, overtime
Child laborStrikes (Pullman, 1894)FLSA limits child labor
Dangerous machines, locked exitsPublic protestSafety laws after the 1911 Triangle fire

notes.say: Factory work in the late 1800s often meant 10 to 12 hours a day, six days a week, children tending machines, and almost no safety rules. One worker who complained could simply be replaced, so workers joined together in unions and bargained as a group. That is collective bargaining, and the strike is the union's strongest tool. At first, government usually sided with employers: in the 1894 Pullman Strike, a federal court ordered the union's leaders to stop interfering with the trains, and President Cleveland sent federal troops to Chicago. That changed during the Great Depression. The Wagner Act of 1935 protected the right to join a union, and the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 set the first federal minimum wage, 25 cents an hour, required overtime pay, and limited child labor.
ask: Why did workers have more power as a union than alone? (Expected: an employer can replace one worker, but not hundreds at once)
Which law set a minimum wage? (Expected: the Fair Labor Standards Act, 1938)
notes.watch: Students mix up the two New Deal laws. Memory hook: Wagner = Workers can organize; FLSA = Floor on pay (minimum wage) and hours.

slides.title: Worked Example: A Cause-and-Effect Chain
slides.board:
"On March 25, 1911, fire broke out at the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory in New York City. Some exit doors had been locked, and 146 workers, most of them young immigrant women, died. Public anger was enormous. Within a few years, New York State passed dozens of new fire-safety and workplace laws."

Build the chain. What was one cause of the deaths, and what was an effect of the fire?
steps: Find the event in the middle: the fire and the 146 deaths.
Look back for causes: locked exit doors (a lack of safety rules) made the deaths worse.
Look forward for effects: public anger → New York passed dozens of new safety laws.
Chain: few safety rules → locked doors → 146 deaths → public anger → new safety laws. GED cause-and-effect questions usually test one link of a chain like this.

notes.say: Teach the student to draw a chain with arrows. Causes come before the event; effects come after. Signal words help: "because," "led to," "as a result," "soon," "after." Then warn them: on the GED, a wrong answer often names something that happened in the same story but is not connected by the text.
ask: Which words in the passage signal an effect? (Expected: "Within a few years" and "passed")
notes.watch: Some students say "the fire caused the factory to be dangerous." Reverse it: the danger existed first and made the fire deadly.

slides.title: We Do: Industry and Labor
slides.board:
1. Put the chain in order: (a) cities grow crowded; (b) factories open and need workers; (c) reformers demand housing and safety laws; (d) farm families move to cities.
  2. In 1937, a 13-year-old works 60 hours a week in a mill. Which later law addressed this?
  3. One worker asks for a raise and is fired. Five hundred workers ask through their union and win. What is this process called, and why did it work?
steps: 1. b → d → a → c. Factories need workers, so families move, so cities crowd, so reformers push for laws.
2. The Fair Labor Standards Act (1938), which limited child labor and long hours.
3. Collective bargaining. An employer can replace one worker but not five hundred at once, so the group has more bargaining power.

notes.say: Work these together. Have the student talk through each link before you reveal it: "first this, so then that." For number 3, push for the reason, not just the term, because the GED asks why unions formed more often than it asks for the definition.
ask: For number 1, which event has to come first, and why? (Expected: factories opening, because nothing else happens until there are jobs)
notes.answer: 1. b, d, a, c. 2. Fair Labor Standards Act (1938). 3. Collective bargaining; the group cannot easily be replaced, so it has more power.
notes.watch: In number 2, students may say "the Wagner Act." Ask: "Is this about forming a union or about limits on work?" Limits on child labor and hours are the FLSA.

slides.title: Trade: Opportunity Cost and Comparative Advantage
slides.board:
Opportunity cost = what you give up.
Absolute advantage = you can make more.
Comparative advantage = you give up less (lower opportunity cost).

Opportunity cost of 1 X = (amount of Y you could make) ÷ (amount of X you could make)

Rule: Specialize in the good with your lower opportunity cost, then trade. Both sides can gain, even if one side is better at everything.

notes.say: Countries trade because of specialization. Each country does best by focusing on what it gives up the least to make. The British economist David Ricardo explained this in 1817, and it surprises people: even a country that can produce more of everything still gains by specializing and trading. The trap on the GED is absolute advantage. Making more of something does not decide who should make it. What decides it is the opportunity cost: what you give up to make one unit.
ask: A lawyer types faster than her assistant. Should she do her own typing? (Expected: probably not; each hour she types, she gives up an hour of legal work worth much more)
notes.watch: The most common error is dividing in the wrong direction. Say it every time: "To make one of this, how many of the other do I give up?" The good you are pricing goes on the bottom.

slides.title: Worked Example: Pies and Bread
slides.board:
In one hour:

BakerPiesLoaves of bread
Ana48
Ben14

Who has the comparative advantage in pies? In bread?
steps: Absolute advantage: Ana makes more of both (4 > 1 pies; 8 > 4 loaves). That does not settle the question.
Cost of 1 pie: Ana gives up 8 ÷ 4 = 2 loaves. Ben gives up 4 ÷ 1 = 4 loaves. Ana's cost is lower: Ana has the comparative advantage in pies.
Cost of 1 loaf: Ana gives up 4 ÷ 8 = 1/2 pie. Ben gives up 1 ÷ 4 = 1/4 pie. Ben's cost is lower: Ben has the comparative advantage in bread.
Conclusion: Ana specializes in pies, Ben in bread, and they trade. Both can end up with more than they could make alone.

notes.say: Write the division on the board every time and say the sentence: "To make one pie, Ana gives up two loaves." Notice that the two answers always split: if one person has the comparative advantage in one good, the other person has it in the other good. That is a built-in check.
ask: Why should Ana let Ben bake bread, when Ana bakes bread faster? (Expected: every hour Ana spends on bread costs her pies, and her pies are worth more of her time)
notes.watch: If the student says "Ana should do both because she is better at both," point to the costs: Ben gives up only 1/4 pie per loaf, half of what Ana gives up.

slides.title: Trade Barriers and the Trade Balance
slides.board:
ToolWhat it does
TariffA tax on imports
QuotaA limit on how much can be imported
EmbargoA ban on trade with a country

Tariff effects: domestic producers gain · buyers pay more · other countries may retaliate

Exports = sold abroad. Imports = bought from abroad.
Imports > exports = trade deficit. Exports > imports = trade surplus.

notes.say: Governments sometimes limit trade. A tariff is a tax on imports; a quota caps the amount; an embargo stops trade completely. A tariff helps the businesses at home that compete with imports, and their workers, but buyers pay higher prices, and other countries often answer with tariffs of their own. History example: after the Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930 raised U.S. tariffs sharply, other countries retaliated and world trade shrank during the Great Depression. Agreements go the other way: NAFTA in 1994 lowered barriers among the United States, Canada, and Mexico, and the USMCA replaced it in 2020. On the GED, keep it neutral: name who gains and who pays, rather than calling a tariff good or bad.
ask: A tariff is placed on imported shoes. Name one group that gains and one group that pays more. (Expected: U.S. shoe makers and their workers gain; shoe buyers pay more)
notes.watch: Students often think the foreign country pays the tariff. The tax is collected when the goods enter the country, and much of the cost is usually passed on to buyers at home in higher prices.

slides.title: Worked Example: Follow the Tariff
slides.board:
Country X places a 25% tariff on imported bicycles. An importer buys a bicycle abroad for $200.

(a) How much is the tariff on that bicycle?
(b) Who is likely to gain and who is likely to pay more?
(c) Country X exports $80 billion of goods and imports $95 billion. Deficit or surplus, and how much?
steps: (a) 25% of $200 = 0.25 × 200 = $50. The importer now pays $250 to bring the bike in.
(b) Chain: higher import cost → higher store price for imported bikes → shoppers pay more or switch to home-made bikes → domestic bike makers gain; bike buyers pay more.
Possible next link: the other country may retaliate with tariffs on Country X's exports.
(c) Imports are larger: 95 − 80 = a trade deficit of $15 billion.

notes.say: The point of this example is the chain, not the arithmetic. A GED question might ask, "Which group would most likely benefit from this tariff?" and offer the foreign producer, the domestic producer, the consumer, and the importer. Walk the chain and the answer is clear. Part (c) shows the most common trade calculation: subtract the smaller from the larger and name which side is bigger.
ask: Why might the foreign country put its own tariff on Country X's goods? (Expected: to retaliate, or to pressure Country X to remove its tariff)
notes.watch: In (c), some students write "surplus" because they subtract and get a positive number. Ask: "Which is larger, what we sell or what we buy?" Buying more than selling is a deficit.

  1. Which country has the comparative advantage in tents? Show the costs.
  2. A law says no more than 2 million tons of sugar may be imported each year. Tariff, quota, or embargo?

2. A quota: it limits the amount, but does not tax or ban it.

notes.say: Let the student lead. For number 1, make them say the full sentence: "To make one tent, Country X gives up two bikes." Then ask which country should make bikes. For 2, focus on the verb in the law: limit, tax, or ban.
ask: Which country should specialize in bikes? (Expected: Country X; a bike costs X 1/2 tent but costs Y 1 tent)
notes.answer: 1. Country Y (1 bike per tent vs. 2 bikes for X). 2. Quota. 3. Trade deficit of $30 billion.
notes.watch: Watch for "Country X, because it makes more." That is absolute advantage. X makes 5 tents and Y makes 6, but the question is about what each gives up.

slides.title: Map Skills: Parts, Types, and the Grid
slides.board:
Parts: title · legend (key) · compass rose · scale · grid

Types: political (borders, cities) · physical (landforms, water) · thematic (one topic, such as rainfall)

LatitudeLongitude
MeasuresN or S of the equatorE or W of the prime meridian
Range0° to 90°0° to 180°
On a gridup = N, down = Sright = E, left = W

Write latitude first: New Orleans ≈ 30°N, 90°W

notes.say: On any map, read the title, legend, compass rose, and scale before the question. Every flat map distorts something: on a Mercator map, Greenland looks about as big as Africa, but Africa is roughly 14 times larger. Latitude lines run east-west like the rungs of a ladder ("ladder-tude") and tell you how far north or south of the equator you are. Longitude lines are long, running pole to pole, and tell you how far east or west of the prime meridian, the line through Greenwich, England. Always write latitude first and always write the direction letters.
ask: Which coordinate tells you how far north or south a place is? (Expected: latitude)
What is the scale for? (Expected: converting map distance to real distance)
notes.watch: Students trained on (x, y) in math read across first and reverse the numbers. Make them say the letter: anything marked N or S is latitude and comes first.

slides.title: Worked Example: Reading the Grid
slides.board:
On this grid each line is 1°. The horizontal axis is the equator; the vertical axis is the prime meridian.

Give the coordinates of Ashby and name its hemispheres. Then: which town is at 4°S, 2°E?
steps: Ashby, latitude: 5 lines above the equator = 5°N.
Ashby, longitude: 3 lines left of the prime meridian = 3°W.
Write latitude first: Ashby is at 5°N, 3°W, in the Northern and Western Hemispheres (not 3°N, 5°W).
4°S, 2°E: 4 lines down, 2 lines right = Dalton.

notes.say: Touch the point and say the moves out loud: "five up, so five north; three left, so three west." Then write latitude first. For the reverse question, start at the center, move up or down for latitude, then left or right for longitude.
ask: Give Corin's coordinates. (Expected: 2°S, 5°W)
notes.watch: The trap answer is the right numbers in the wrong order (3°N, 5°W) or the right numbers with the wrong letters (5°N, 3°E). Check both every time.

slides.title: We Do: Maps and Coordinates
slides.board:
1. A city is 1 line below the equator and 5 lines right of the prime meridian. Give its coordinates.
  2. A map scale reads 1 inch = 50 miles. Two towns are 3.5 inches apart on the map. How far apart are they?
  3. New Orleans is at about 30°N, 90°W. Which two hemispheres is it in?
  4. A map shows average yearly rainfall in each county by color. Political, physical, or thematic?
steps: 1. 1°S, 5°E (latitude first; not 5°S, 1°E).
2. 3.5 × 50 = 175 miles.
3. Northern (N) and Western (W).
4. Thematic: it shows one topic (rainfall).

notes.say: Do these together quickly. For number 2, have the student write the scale as a multiplication: inches times 50. For number 3, the letters give the hemispheres directly: N or S for one, E or W for the other.
ask: Why is a rainfall map not a physical map, even though rain is part of nature? (Expected: a physical map shows landforms and water features; a map built around one topic is thematic)
notes.watch: On number 2, a few students divide (3.5 ÷ 50). Ask: "Is the real distance bigger or smaller than 3.5 inches?" Bigger, so multiply.

slides.title: Five Themes of Geography
slides.board:
ThemeQuestion it answers
LocationWhere is it? (absolute = coordinates; relative = near what)
PlaceWhat is it like there?
Human-environment interactionHow do people depend on, adapt to, and modify the land?
MovementHow do people, goods, and ideas travel?
RegionWhat area shares a feature? (formal, functional, perceptual)

notes.say: Geographers organize their questions with five themes. Human-environment interaction is the GED favorite: people depend on the environment (farming fertile soil), adapt to it (building houses on stilts in a flood zone), and modify it (Hoover Dam, completed in 1936, blocks the Colorado River for water and power). Regions come in three kinds. A formal region shares a measurable feature, such as a climate zone or the counties where most farmland grows corn. A functional region is organized around a hub, such as the area a TV station or a delivery service covers. A perceptual region is based on how people feel about an area, such as "the Heartland."
ask: A town builds levees along a river to stop floods. Depend, adapt, or modify? (Expected: modify)
The area served by one airport's flights. Formal, functional, or perceptual region? (Expected: functional)
notes.watch: Students call any natural event human-environment interaction. A drought alone is nature. It becomes interaction when people's actions or responses are part of the story.

slides.title: Migration: Push and Pull
slides.board:
Push (reasons to leave)

  • War or violence
  • Drought, famine, lost farms
  • Persecution, unfair laws
  • No jobs

Pull (reasons to go)

  • Jobs and higher wages
  • Safety and freedom
  • Family already there
  • Available land

Test: Is it about the old place (push) or the new place (pull)?

Great Migration (about 1910–1970): roughly 6 million African Americans leave the rural South for cities in the North, Midwest, and West.

notes.say: Migration is moving to a new home. Push factors drive people out of the old place; pull factors draw them to the new one. Most moves have both. In the Great Migration, segregation laws, racial violence, and failing cotton farms in the South were push factors; factory jobs in cities like Chicago and Detroit, which grew during World War I when European immigration dropped, were pull factors. Not all migration is voluntary: the Atlantic slave trade and the Cherokee Trail of Tears in 1838 and 1839 were forced migrations.
ask: Relatives in the new city offer to share their apartment. Push or pull? (Expected: pull, because it makes the new place attractive)
notes.watch: Students sometimes call family a push factor because "family made them go." Use the test: is it a problem with the old place or an attraction of the new place?

slides.title: Worked Example: The Dust Bowl
slides.board:
"In the 1910s and 1920s, high wheat prices and new tractors led Great Plains farmers to plow up millions of acres of deep-rooted grassland. In the early 1930s a severe drought struck. With the grass gone, strong winds blew the dry soil into huge dust storms. Many families lost their farms, and hundreds of thousands left, many for farm work in California. In 1935, Congress created the Soil Conservation Service."

Show the human-environment interaction. Then name one push and one pull factor.
steps: People modify the land: farmers plowed up the grasses that held the soil.
The land affects people: during the drought, nothing held the soil; dust storms ruined farms.
People respond: families migrated, and the new Soil Conservation Service taught farmers to change how they farmed (windbreaks, crop rotation, plowing along the land's curves).
Push: ruined farms and dust storms on the Plains. Pull: the hope of farm work in California.

notes.say: This is the model GED human-environment interaction story because it runs both ways: people changed the land, and the changed land changed people's lives. The drought was natural, but the passage makes clear that plowing up the grass made the damage far worse. Have the student point to the words that prove each link.
ask: Which words prove that farming practices played a part? (Expected: "With the grass gone")
notes.watch: The tempting wrong answer is "the drought alone caused the dust storms." The passage connects the storms to the missing grass.

slides.title: We Do: Themes, Regions, and Migration
slides.board:
1. The area that receives deliveries from one city's pizza shop. Formal, functional, or perceptual region?
  2. Farmers carve flat steps (terraces) into steep hillsides to grow rice. Depend, adapt, or modify?
  3. Push or pull? (a) the boll weevil destroys Southern cotton crops; (b) Detroit auto plants hire workers during World War I; (c) segregation laws in the South.
steps: 1. Functional: it is organized around a hub (the shop).
2. Modify: the farmers change the shape of the land.
3. (a) push; (b) pull; (c) push. Only (b) is about the new place.

notes.say: Read each one aloud and have the student name the category and give the reason before you reveal. For number 2, contrast modify and adapt: adapting means changing yourself or your behavior to fit the land; modifying means changing the land.
ask: Give an example of adapting to a hot desert. (Expected: thick-walled houses, working in the cooler hours, light clothing)
notes.watch: For the boll weevil, students may say "human-environment interaction" instead of push or pull. It can be both. Here the question asks push or pull, so answer that.

slides.title: You Do 1: Industry and Labor
slides.board:
On your own (4 minutes).

  1. Put in order: Triangle fire; Erie Canal opens; Fair Labor Standards Act; transcontinental railroad completed.
  2. Which 1935 law protected workers' right to form unions?
  3. Urban share: 35.1% in 1890, 45.6% in 1910. Change in percentage points?
  4. Give one reason factory workers formed unions.
steps: 1. Erie Canal (1825) → railroad (1869) → Triangle fire (1911) → FLSA (1938). 2. The Wagner Act (National Labor Relations Act). 3. 45.6 − 35.1 = 10.5 percentage points. 4. To bargain as a group for better pay, shorter hours, or safer conditions, because one worker alone could easily be replaced.

notes.say: Start a four-minute timer and stay quiet. When time is up, have the student give all four answers before you reveal. For number 4, accept any answer that includes acting as a group for better pay, hours, or safety.
ask: For number 1, which date helped you most? (Expected: any; check that they know at least the canal and the FLSA)
notes.answer: 1. Erie Canal, railroad, Triangle fire, FLSA. 2. Wagner Act (1935). 3. 10.5 percentage points. 4. Bargaining power as a group for pay, hours, or safety.

slides.title: You Do 3: Maps and Geography
slides.board:
On your own (4 minutes).

  1. A point is 4 lines below the equator and 2 lines right of the prime meridian. Coordinates?
  2. Buenos Aires, Argentina, is at about 35°S, 58°W. Which hemispheres?
  3. The area that gets home delivery of one city's newspaper. Formal, functional, or perceptual region?
  4. Push or pull? (a) famine in the home country; (b) a cousin offers a job in the new city.
steps: 1. 4°S, 2°E. 2. Southern and Western. 3. Functional (organized around the newspaper as a hub). 4. (a) push; (b) pull.

notes.say: Four minutes on the clock. When the student reports, ask for the reason on numbers 3 and 4, not just the label.
ask: For number 1, what would the wrong answer "2°S, 4°E" mean? (Expected: the numbers were read in x, y order instead of latitude first)
notes.answer: 1. 4°S, 2°E. 2. Southern and Western. 3. Functional. 4. (a) push, (b) pull.

Which conclusion is supported by the table?

A. Delmar should make both goods, because its workers produce more of each.
B. Kesh has a comparative advantage in phones, because it gives up fewer shirts to make each phone.
C. Delmar has a comparative advantage in phones, because its workers make 10 phones and Kesh's make only 6.
D. Neither country can gain from trade, because Delmar is more productive in both goods.
steps: Find the costs first. 1 phone costs Delmar 30 ÷ 10 = 3 shirts; it costs Kesh 12 ÷ 6 = 2 shirts.
Eliminate A. Producing more of each is absolute advantage. Specializing by lower opportunity cost lets both countries gain.
Eliminate C. 10 vs. 6 phones is absolute advantage. Delmar gives up 3 shirts per phone, more than Kesh's 2.
Eliminate D. This is the classic misconception. Countries gain from trade whenever their opportunity costs differ, as they do here.
Answer B. Kesh gives up 2 shirts per phone; Delmar gives up 3. Lower opportunity cost = comparative advantage.

notes.say: Have the student compute both costs before reading the choices. Then eliminate out loud. Three of the four choices are built on the same mistake, confusing "makes more" with "gives up less." Once the student sees that pattern, these questions get fast.
ask: Which country has the comparative advantage in shirts? (Expected: Delmar; a shirt costs Delmar 1/3 phone and Kesh 1/2 phone)
notes.answer: B. Kesh has a comparative advantage in phones (2 shirts per phone vs. 3 for Delmar).
notes.watch: C is the trap: it uses a true number from the table. Ask: "Does 'makes more' tell you what is given up?"

slides.title: GED Question 2: Reading Labor Data
slides.board:
The graph shows the share of U.S. wage and salary workers who belonged to labor unions (Bureau of Labor Statistics).

Which statement is supported by the graph?

A. The union membership rate in 2023 was about half the rate in 1983.
B. The number of union members went down in every year from 1983 to 2023.
C. The membership rate fell because new federal laws made it harder to join a union.
D. The membership rate will fall below 5 percent by the 2040s.

figure.title: Union Members as a Percent of U.S. Wage and Salary Workers

steps: Read the labels. The bars show a rate (percent of workers), measured once every ten years.
Eliminate B. The graph shows the rate, not the number of members, and it shows only five years, not every year.
Eliminate C. The graph shows that the rate fell, not why. Nothing on it is about laws.
Eliminate D. This is a prediction. The data stop at 2023.
Answer A. 1983: 20.1%. 2023: 10.0%. Half of 20.1 is about 10, so the rate was cut roughly in half.

notes.say: Teach the student to check three things a graph cannot do: it cannot show what it does not measure (here, the number of members), it cannot explain why, and it cannot see the future. Words like "because," "every year," and "will" are red flags on data questions.
ask: By how many percentage points did the rate fall from 1983 to 2023? (Expected: 20.1 − 10.0 = 10.1 points)
notes.answer: A. The rate fell from 20.1% to 10.0%, about half.
notes.watch: B is tempting because the bars go down. Ask: "Is this graph about how many people, or what percent of workers? And does it show every year?"

slides.title: GED Strategy: Work It Out Before You Look
slides.board:
1. Read the question first, then the stimulus.
  2. Do the work on scratch paper first: write the coordinates with letters, or the opportunity costs with the division shown.
  3. Then match your answer to the choices.
  4. Check both parts: right numbers and right letters; right country and right reason.
  5. Eliminate "makes more" reasons, causes a graph cannot show, and predictions.

Pace: about 2 minutes per question on our practice tests.

notes.say: Trade and map questions are built so that every wrong answer looks like a real answer: the right numbers with the wrong letters, the right country with the wrong reason. If the student reads the choices first, those traps pull them in. If they work the answer out first, they walk in already knowing what they are looking for. On the real GED there is an erasable note board for exactly this.
ask: What two things should you check on a coordinate answer? (Expected: the numbers in latitude-first order and the direction letters)
notes.watch: Strong students skip the written step because it "feels slow." Time them once: writing two divisions takes about 20 seconds and prevents the most common errors.

screens.title: What You Will Learn
screens.html:
About 15 percent of the GED Social Studies test is economics and about 15 percent is geography, and many history questions are really about money, work, and trade. This lesson connects three big stories from U.S. history (factories, workers, and trade) and gives you the map and geography skills that GED questions use.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Explain how industrialization changed work, cities, and the U.S. economy, and trace cause-and-effect chains
  • Describe why workers formed labor unions and how government responded
  • Use opportunity cost and comparative advantage to explain trade, and predict the effects of tariffs
  • Locate places with latitude and longitude and name hemispheres and directions
  • Apply the themes of geography, including regions, human-environment interaction, and push and pull factors in migration

Each screen teaches one idea and ends with a quick check. Answer it before you move on.

screens.title: Industrialization: From Hand to Machine
screens.html:
Industrialization is the change from making goods by hand to making them with machines in factories. It began in Great Britain in the late 1700s and reached the United States around 1790, when a British-trained mechanic named Samuel Slater helped start a water-powered cotton-spinning mill in Pawtucket, Rhode Island.

Starting in the 1820s, large textile mills in Lowell, Massachusetts, hired young women from New England farms; by the 1830s thousands worked there. After the Civil War, steel (led by Andrew Carnegie) and oil (led by John D. Rockefeller) became giant industries. In 1890 Congress passed the Sherman Antitrust Act to outlaw business combinations that limited competition.

Main effects: goods became cheaper; millions of factory jobs appeared; people moved from farms to cities to take them.

check.prompt: Which statement describes an effect of industrialization in the United States?
options: Many people moved from farms to cities to work in factories.
Most goods came to be made by hand in homes and small shops.
Factory jobs drew large numbers of workers out of cities.
Machine-made cloth became more costly than handmade cloth.
why: This reverses the change. Industrialization moved production out of homes and small shops and into machine-powered factories.
This reverses the direction of movement. Factories were in towns and cities, so jobs pulled people into cities, not out of them.
Machines made goods cheaper, not more costly. Lower prices are one reason factory goods replaced handmade ones.
check.hint: Think about where factories were built and who worked in them.
check.explain: Factories needed large numbers of workers, and they were located in towns and cities. So industrialization pulled people from farms to cities. The other choices reverse what happened: production moved out of homes, people moved into cities, and machine-made goods became cheaper.

screens.title: Transportation and the Growth of Cities
screens.html:
Factories could only grow if they could ship goods to buyers far away. Two projects changed that:

  • Erie Canal (1825): linked the Hudson River at Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo, so goods could travel by water between the Great Lakes and New York City. Shipping costs fell sharply, and New York City became the nation's leading port.
  • Transcontinental railroad (1869): joined the East and West by rail at Promontory Summit, Utah.

As factories and transportation grew, so did cities. The graph shows census data on the share of Americans living in urban areas (places with 2,500 or more people). The 1920 census was the first to count more than half of Americans as urban.

Points vs. percent: when you subtract two percentages, the answer is in percentage points.

figure.title: Percent of U.S. Population Living in Urban Areas

example.prompt: Using the graph, by how many percentage points did the urban share rise from 1880 to 1920?
steps: Subtract: 51.2 − 28.2 = 23.0.

check.prompt: Using the graph, by how many percentage points did the urban share of the U.S. population rise from 1860 to 1900?

mistakes.why: You started from the 1870 value (39.6 − 25.7). The question starts at 1860: 39.6 − 19.8.
That is the percent increase (the share doubled). The question asks for percentage points, so just subtract: 39.6 − 19.8.
You added the two values. To find how much the share rose, subtract the earlier value from the later one.

check.hint: Find the 1860 and 1900 points on the line, then subtract.
check.explain:
1900 value: 39.6%
1860 value: 19.8%
Change: 39.6 − 19.8 = 19.8 percentage points.

Notice that the 1900 share is exactly double the 1860 share, a 100 percent increase. That is a different measure: the question asks for percentage points, so subtract.

screens.title: Why Workers Organized
screens.html:
Early factory jobs often meant 10 to 12 hours a day, six days a week, low pay, children working at machines, and few safety guards. A worker who complained could simply be replaced, because many people were looking for work.

So workers joined together in labor unions. A union bargains with the employer for all of its members at once. This is called collective bargaining. If talks fail, the union may call a strike, meaning the members refuse to work. The American Federation of Labor (AFL), led by Samuel Gompers, was founded in 1886.

At first, government often sided with employers. In the Pullman Strike of 1894, railroad workers stopped trains across much of the country to support factory workers whose wages had been cut. A federal court ordered the union's leaders to stop, and President Grover Cleveland sent federal troops to Chicago. The strike collapsed.

check.prompt: Read the account of a fictional mill. Click the sentence that best explains why the workers formed a union.
spans: In 1890, the Riverton Mill cut the pay of its 400 weavers by one-fifth.
Weaver Ada Holt asked the manager to restore her pay, and she was fired the next day.
The other weavers decided that the mill could fire one complaining worker but could not replace all 400 at once.
They formed the Riverton Weavers' Union and elected Holt as its first president.
The mill's owner later built a new dye house beside the river.
check.why: The most common wrong click is the sentence about the pay cut. The pay cut is the problem that started the story, but the reason they chose a union is the sentence about the group being impossible to replace all at once.
check.hint: Look for the sentence that explains the workers' thinking, not the sentence that describes the problem.
check.explain:
The workers' reasoning is stated directly: the mill "could fire one complaining worker but could not replace all 400 at once." That is the logic of collective bargaining: a group has bargaining power that one worker lacks.

The pay cut and Holt's firing are the background problem, and forming the union is the action, not the reason for it.

screens.title: Government Responds to Labor Problems
screens.html:
Public opinion began to change after the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire in New York City on March 25, 1911. Some exit doors were locked, and 146 workers, most of them young immigrant women, died. New York soon passed dozens of fire-safety and workplace laws.

During the Great Depression, the federal government acted:

LawWhat it did
National Labor Relations Act (Wagner Act), 1935Protected workers' right to form unions and bargain collectively
Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), 1938Set a federal minimum wage (25 cents an hour at first), required overtime pay beyond a standard workweek, and restricted child labor

Memory hook: Wagner = Workers may organize. FLSA = a Floor under pay and limits on hours.

check.prompt:
Complete the statements.

A law passed in 1935 that protected workers' right to join a union and bargain with their employer was the {{0}}.

A law passed in 1938 that set a federal minimum wage and limited child labor was the {{1}}.

options: Wagner Act
Fair Labor Standards Act
Sherman Antitrust Act
Social Security Act
why: The FLSA (1938) set wages and hours. The right to organize came from the 1935 Wagner Act.
The Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) outlawed business combinations that limited competition. It is not a labor-rights law.
The Social Security Act (1935) created old-age insurance, not the right to form unions.

options: Fair Labor Standards Act
Wagner Act
Sherman Antitrust Act
Social Security Act
why: The Wagner Act (1935) protected the right to organize. It did not set a minimum wage.
The Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) is about business competition, not wages or child labor.
The Social Security Act created retirement insurance; it did not set a minimum wage.

check.hint: Use the memory hook: W for Workers organize, F for a Floor under pay.
check.explain:
Blank 1: Wagner Act (National Labor Relations Act, 1935): the right to organize and bargain collectively.

Blank 2: Fair Labor Standards Act (1938): minimum wage, overtime pay, and limits on child labor. Students often swap the two; use the hook "Wagner = workers organize; FLSA = floor on pay."

screens.title: Opportunity Cost: The Key to Trade
screens.html:
Last week you learned that opportunity cost is what you give up when you choose one thing over another. Countries face the same choice: a worker who spends the day making one good is not making another.

Opportunity cost of 1 unit of X = (amount of Y that could be made) ÷ (amount of X that could be made)

Say the sentence every time: "To make one of this, I give up ___ of that." The good you are pricing goes on the bottom of the division.

Example: A worker can make 12 shirts or 4 radios in a day. To make 1 radio, she gives up 12 ÷ 4 = 3 shirts. To make 1 shirt, she gives up 4 ÷ 12 = 1/3 of a radio.

check.prompt: In one month, a worker in Country K can produce either 20 tons of corn or 5 tractors. What is the opportunity cost of producing 1 tractor, in tons of corn?

mistakes.why: You divided in the wrong direction (5 ÷ 20). That is the cost of 1 ton of corn in tractors. For 1 tractor, put tractors on the bottom: 20 ÷ 5.
You subtracted (20 − 5). Opportunity cost per unit comes from dividing: 20 tons ÷ 5 tractors.
20 tons is what the worker gives up to make all 5 tractors. For one tractor, divide: 20 ÷ 5.

check.hint: To make ONE tractor, how many tons of corn are given up? Put tractors on the bottom.
check.explain:
To make 5 tractors, the worker gives up 20 tons of corn. For 1 tractor: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 tons of corn.

The answer 0.25 comes from dividing the other way, which gives the cost of a ton of corn in tractors.

screens.title: Comparative Advantage
screens.html:
Two ideas sound alike but mean different things:

  • Absolute advantage: you can make more of a good with the same resources.
  • Comparative advantage: you give up less to make it (a lower opportunity cost).

The British economist David Ricardo showed in 1817 that countries should specialize in the goods they have a comparative advantage in and then trade. Both sides gain, even when one country can produce more of everything.

example.prompt: In one week, a worker in Alta can make 20 shirts or 10 radios. A worker in Bora can make 12 shirts or 4 radios. Which country has the comparative advantage in radios?
steps: Cost of 1 radio in Alta: 20 ÷ 10 = 2 shirts. In Bora: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 shirts.
Alta gives up fewer shirts per radio, so Alta has the comparative advantage in radios.
Check the other good: 1 shirt costs Alta 1/2 radio but costs Bora only 1/3 radio, so Bora has the comparative advantage in shirts.
example.answer: Alta has the comparative advantage in radios; Bora has it in shirts.

check.prompt: In one day, a worker in Pell can build 9 chairs or 3 tables. A worker in Quin can build 4 chairs or 2 tables. Which country has the comparative advantage in tables, and why?
options: Quin, because each table costs it 2 chairs instead of 3
Pell, because its workers build 3 tables a day instead of 2
Pell, because each table costs it only 1/3 of a chair
Quin, because its workers build fewer chairs than Pell's do
why: Building more tables is absolute advantage. Compare what each country gives up: Pell gives up 3 chairs per table, Quin only 2.
You divided in the wrong direction (3 ÷ 9). That is the cost of a chair in tables. One table costs Pell 9 ÷ 3 = 3 chairs.
Quin is the right country, but for the wrong reason. Making fewer chairs is not the test; the test is the lower opportunity cost, 2 chairs per table.
check.hint: Find what 1 table costs each country in chairs. Lower cost wins.
check.explain:
Cost of 1 table: Pell gives up 9 ÷ 3 = 3 chairs; Quin gives up 4 ÷ 2 = 2 chairs. Quin gives up less, so Quin has the comparative advantage in tables.

Pell builds more tables (3 vs. 2), but that is absolute advantage, which does not decide who should specialize.

screens.title: Tariffs, Quotas, and Embargoes
screens.html:
Governments sometimes limit trade with three main tools:

  • Tariff: a tax on imports.
  • Quota: a limit on how much of a good can be imported.
  • Embargo: a ban on trade with a country.

Follow the chain for a tariff: the tax raises the cost of imported goods → prices for those goods rise → buyers pay more or switch to goods made at home → domestic producers that compete with the imports (and their workers) gain, while buyers pay more. Other countries may retaliate with tariffs of their own.

After the Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930 raised U.S. tariffs sharply, other countries retaliated and world trade shrank during the Great Depression. Free-trade agreements lower barriers instead: NAFTA (1994) among the United States, Canada, and Mexico was replaced by the USMCA in 2020.

check.prompt: Drag each policy into the correct category.
choices: A 15 percent tax is charged on every imported television.
No more than 50,000 imported cars may enter the country each year.
All trade with a neighboring country is banned after an invasion.
Importers pay $3 to the government for each pair of foreign shoes.
Only 1 million tons of foreign sugar may be imported per year.
check.why: The most common mistake is putting the sugar limit under tariff. A quota limits the amount of a good; a tariff charges a tax on it.
check.hint: Ask: Is it a tax, a limit on the amount, or a complete ban?
check.explain:
• Tariff (a tax): the 15 percent tax on televisions and the $3 charge per pair of shoes.
  • Quota (a limit on amount): the 50,000-car limit and the 1-million-ton sugar limit.
  • Embargo (a ban): stopping all trade with the neighboring country.

screens.title: Exports, Imports, and the Trade Balance
screens.html:
Exports are goods and services a country sells to other countries. Imports are goods and services it buys from them.

Trade balance = exports − imports
Imports larger than exports → trade deficit
Exports larger than imports → trade surplus

To find the size of a deficit or surplus, subtract the smaller number from the larger one, then name which side is bigger.

example.prompt: Country X exports $80 billion of goods and imports $95 billion. Find its trade balance.
steps: Which is larger? Imports ($95 billion).
Subtract: 95 − 80 = 15.

check.prompt: Last year, the fictional country of Ostria exported $62 billion of goods and imported $85 billion. How large was Ostria's trade deficit, in billions of dollars?

mistakes.why: You added exports and imports. The trade balance is the difference: 85 − 62.
You divided imports by exports. A trade deficit is a difference in dollars, so subtract: 85 − 62.

check.hint: Subtract the smaller number from the larger one.
check.explain:
Imports ($85 billion) are larger than exports ($62 billion), so Ostria has a deficit.
85 − 62 = $23 billion.

screens.title: Reading Maps: Parts and Types
screens.html:
Before you answer any map question, check these parts:

  • Title: what the map is about.
  • Legend (key): what the symbols and colors mean.
  • Compass rose: north, south, east, and west.
  • Scale: how map distance compares to real distance. Multiply: map inches × miles per inch.

A political map shows borders and cities. A physical map shows landforms and water. A thematic map shows one topic, such as rainfall, population, or election results.

Every flat map distorts something. On a Mercator map, Greenland looks about as large as Africa, but Africa is roughly 14 times larger.

check.prompt: A map's scale reads 1 inch = 40 miles. Two towns are 4.5 inches apart on the map. How many miles apart are they?

mistakes.why: You added the two numbers. A scale tells you how many miles each inch stands for, so multiply: 4.5 × 40.
You divided 40 by 4.5. The real distance is larger than the map distance, so multiply: 4.5 × 40.
That is 4 inches only. Include the half inch: 4.5 × 40 = 180.

check.hint: Each inch on the map stands for 40 real miles.

screens.title: Latitude and Longitude
screens.html:
Mapmakers use a grid of imaginary lines to give every place an exact address, its absolute location.

LatitudeLongitude
MeasuresDistance north or south of the equatorDistance east or west of the prime meridian (through Greenwich, England)
Range0° to 90° N or S0° to 180° E or W
On a gridup = N, down = Sright = E, left = W
Memory trickLike the rungs of a ladder ("ladder-tude")Lines are long, pole to pole

Rule: write latitude first, then longitude, always with direction letters. New Orleans is at about 30°N, 90°W.

example.prompt: On the grid (each line = 1°; the horizontal axis is the equator and the vertical axis is the prime meridian), give Ashby's coordinates.
steps: Latitude: Ashby is 5 lines above the equator: 5°N.
Longitude: Ashby is 3 lines left of the prime meridian: 3°W.
Write latitude first.

check.prompt: On the grid, the horizontal axis is the equator and the vertical axis is the prime meridian. Each line is 1 degree. Click the point at 3°S, 4°W.
check.why: The most common wrong click is 4 lines down and 3 lines left, which reads the numbers in x, y order. The S tells you 3 is the latitude, so move 3 lines down first.
check.hint: Start where the axes cross. The S number moves you down; the W number moves you left.
check.explain:
3°S is latitude: move 3 lines down from the equator. 4°W is longitude: move 4 lines left of the prime meridian. The point is 4 left and 3 down.

Clicking 3 left and 4 down reverses latitude and longitude; that point would be 4°S, 3°W.

screens.title: Hemispheres and Direction
screens.html:
The equator splits Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. The prime meridian (with the 180° line on the other side of the world) splits it into the Eastern and Western Hemispheres. The direction letters tell you the hemispheres directly: N or S for one, E or W for the other.

To describe a trip between two places, compare their coordinates:

  • If the latitude moves from S toward N, the trip goes north (and crosses the equator if the letter changes).
  • If the longitude moves from E toward W, the trip goes west (and crosses the prime meridian if the letter changes).

Example: From 2°S, 4°E to 2°N, 4°W, the trip goes northwest and crosses both the equator and the prime meridian.

check.prompt: Sydney, Australia, is located at about 34°S, 151°E. In which two hemispheres is Sydney?
options: Southern and Eastern
Northern and Eastern
Southern and Western
Northern and Western
why: The S in 34°S means south of the equator, so Sydney is in the Southern Hemisphere, not the Northern.
The E in 151°E means east of the prime meridian, so Sydney is in the Eastern Hemisphere, not the Western.
Both letters were flipped. S means Southern and E means Eastern.
check.hint: Each direction letter names one hemisphere.
check.explain: The letters answer the question: S = Southern Hemisphere and E = Eastern Hemisphere.

screens.title: The Five Themes and Three Kinds of Regions
screens.html:
Geographers organize their questions with five themes:

  1. Location: where a place is. Absolute location uses coordinates; relative location uses nearby places ("just south of the river").
  2. Place: what a place is like (land, climate, people, culture).
  3. Human-environment interaction: how people depend on, adapt to, and change the environment.
  4. Movement: how people, goods, and ideas travel.
  5. Region: an area that shares a feature.

There are three kinds of regions. A formal region shares a measurable feature (a climate zone, the counties where most farmland is planted in corn). A functional region is organized around a hub (a city's bus system, an airport's flight area). A perceptual region is based on people's feelings or beliefs (the "Heartland").

check.prompt: Drag each example into the type of region it describes.
choices: The area served by one city's bus system
Counties where more than half the land is forest
The part of the country many people call "the Heartland"
The neighborhoods that one hospital's ambulances serve
Places where the average January temperature is below freezing
check.why: The most common mistake is putting the bus system or the ambulance area under formal region. Those areas are defined by a hub that serves them, which makes them functional.
check.hint: Ask how the border is drawn: by a measurement, by a hub, or by people's opinions?
check.explain:
• Formal (shared measurable feature): forest-covered counties; places with average January temperatures below freezing.
  • Functional (organized around a hub): the bus system's area; the hospital's ambulance area.
  • Perceptual (based on feelings): "the Heartland," which has no agreed-upon border.

screens.title: Human-Environment Interaction
screens.html:
People interact with their environment in three ways:

WayMeaningExample
DependUse what nature providesFishing in a river; farming fertile soil
AdaptChange behavior or buildings to fit the environmentHouses on stilts in a flood zone; heavy coats in a cold climate
ModifyChange the environment itselfHoover Dam (completed 1936) blocks the Colorado River for water and power; levees; irrigation canals

A natural event alone (a hurricane, a drought) is not human-environment interaction. It becomes one when people's actions or responses are part of the story.

check.prompt: Which is an example of people adapting to their environment?
options: Families in a flood-prone area build their homes on tall stilts.
Engineers build a dam across a river to create a reservoir.
A fishing village catches and sells fish from a nearby lake.
A powerful hurricane floods dozens of towns along the coast.
why: Building a dam changes the river itself. That is modifying the environment, not adapting to it.
Using the lake's fish for food and income is depending on the environment.
A hurricane is a natural event. No human action or response is described, so it is not an example of adapting.
check.hint: Adapting means people change themselves or how they build. Modifying means they change the land or water.
check.explain: Building homes on stilts changes how people build so that they fit the environment, without changing the river or the flooding. That is adapting. The dam is modifying, the fishing village is depending, and the hurricane alone is a natural event.

screens.title: Migration: Push and Pull
screens.html:
Migration is moving to a new home. People leave because of push factors and choose a destination because of pull factors.

Push (reasons to leave)

  • War or violence
  • Drought, famine, or lost farms
  • Persecution or unfair laws
  • No jobs

Pull (reasons to go)

  • Jobs and higher wages
  • Safety and freedom
  • Family already there
  • Available land

Some migration is forced, such as the Atlantic slave trade and the removal of the Cherokee on the Trail of Tears (1838–1839).

example.prompt: In the Great Migration (about 1910–1970), roughly 6 million African Americans moved from the rural South to cities in the North, Midwest, and West. Is "segregation laws in the South" a push or a pull factor?
steps: Ask: is it about the old place or the new place?
Segregation laws describe the South, the place people left.
example.answer: A push factor. Factory jobs in cities such as Chicago and Detroit would be pull factors.

check.prompt: Marcus Reed left a small Mississippi farm town for Chicago in 1917. Which details describe push factors? Select two answers.
options: The boll weevil had destroyed most of the cotton crop on his family's farm.
A meatpacking plant in Chicago was hiring workers at higher wages.
Segregation laws in his town kept him out of the public library.
His older sister already had an apartment on Chicago's South Side.
A Chicago newspaper described jobs and schools waiting in the North.
why: Higher-paying jobs in Chicago are an attraction of the new place, so this is a pull factor.
A sister with an apartment makes Chicago more attractive. Family at the destination is a pull factor.
The newspaper describes opportunities in the North, the new place. That is a pull factor.
check.hint: Ask of each detail: is it about Mississippi (the old place) or Chicago (the new place)?
check.explain:
Push factors are problems in the place people leave. Two details describe Mississippi: the boll weevil destroying the cotton crop and the segregation laws in his town.

The meatpacking jobs, his sister's apartment, and the newspaper's description of the North are all about Chicago, so they are pull factors.

screens.title: Putting It Together: One Chain, Four Topics
screens.html:
GED questions often link economics, history, and geography in one cause-and-effect chain. Here is one that uses everything in this lesson:

  1. Industry and transportation: railroads reached the Great Plains, so farmers could ship wheat to distant cities.
  2. Economics: in the 1910s and 1920s, high wheat prices and new gasoline tractors made plowing more land profitable.
  3. Human-environment interaction: farmers plowed up millions of acres of deep-rooted grass that had held the soil.
  4. Nature and people together: a severe drought in the early 1930s turned the bare soil into the dust storms of the Dust Bowl.
  5. Migration: ruined farms pushed hundreds of thousands of people off the Plains, many to California.

In 1935, Congress created the Soil Conservation Service to teach farmers to plant windbreaks, rotate crops, and plow along the land's curves.

check.prompt: In the chain on this screen, which event is the best example of people modifying the environment?
options: Farmers plowed up the deep-rooted grass that held the soil.
A severe drought struck the southern Plains in the early 1930s.
Families left the Plains and moved west to look for work.
Wheat prices rose sharply during the 1910s and 1920s.
why: A drought is a natural event. People did not cause the lack of rain, so it is not people modifying the land.
Moving away is migration, a response to the damaged land. It does not change the environment itself.
High wheat prices are an economic cause that encouraged plowing, but a price is not a change to the land.
check.hint: Which event shows people physically changing the land?
check.explain: Plowing up the grass changed the land itself, which is modifying the environment. The drought was natural, the move west was migration, and wheat prices were the economic cause that encouraged the plowing.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• Industrialization: hand to machine production. U.S. textile mills from about 1790; Erie Canal 1825; transcontinental railroad 1869. Effects: cheaper goods, factory jobs, urban growth (urban majority first counted in 1920).
  • Labor: long hours, low pay, child labor, danger → unions, collective bargaining, strikes (AFL 1886; Pullman 1894). Triangle fire 1911 → safety laws. Wagner Act 1935 (right to organize); FLSA 1938 (minimum wage, overtime, child labor limits).
  • Trade: opportunity cost = what you give up. Comparative advantage = lower opportunity cost; specialize and trade. Tariff = tax on imports (domestic producers gain, buyers pay more); quota = limit; embargo = ban. Imports > exports = deficit.
  • Maps: title, legend, compass rose, scale. Latitude (N/S of the equator) first, then longitude (E/W of the prime meridian), always with letters.
  • Geography: location, place, human-environment interaction (depend, adapt, modify), movement, region (formal, functional, perceptual). Push = reason to leave; pull = reason to go.

Next: the Practice set. Read every explanation, even on questions you get right.

stimuli.title: Reading: Factories, Workers, and Reform
stimuli.html:
(1) In the early 1800s, most Americans worked on farms or in small shops. Over the next hundred years, machines powered first by water and later by steam and electricity moved much of the nation's production into large factories. Factories could make cloth, shoes, and steel far more cheaply than skilled workers could by hand, and prices for many goods fell.

(2) For workers, however, the change came with a cost. A typical factory employee in the late 1800s worked 10 to 12 hours a day, six days a week. Children, many of them younger than 14, tended machines in textile mills and sorted coal in mines. Machines had few safety guards, and workers who lost fingers or hands in accidents usually received no payment from their employers.

(3) Because one worker could easily be replaced, many workers decided that they had a better chance of winning higher pay and safer conditions if they acted together. They formed labor unions, which bargained with employers on behalf of all their members. The American Federation of Labor, founded in 1886, became the largest union organization of its time. When bargaining failed, unions sometimes called strikes.

(4) Public opinion began to shift after a disaster in New York City. On March 25, 1911, a fire broke out at the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory. Some exit doors had been locked, and 146 workers, most of them young immigrant women, died. New York State soon passed dozens of new fire-safety and workplace laws.

(5) The federal government acted during the Great Depression. The National Labor Relations Act of 1935 protected workers' right to form unions. The Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 set a national minimum wage, required overtime pay for long workweeks, and restricted child labor.

stimuli.title: Reading: The Dust Bowl
stimuli.html:
The southern Great Plains, including parts of Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, Colorado, and New Mexico, was once covered by deep-rooted prairie grasses. These grasses held the soil in place through dry spells and strong winds.

In the 1910s and 1920s, high wheat prices and new gasoline-powered tractors encouraged farmers to plow millions of acres of this grassland and plant wheat. For several years, rainfall was good and harvests were large.

Then, in the early 1930s, a severe drought struck. With the grass gone and the crops dying, nothing held the dry topsoil. Strong winds lifted it into enormous dust storms. On April 14, 1935, remembered as "Black Sunday," a wall of dust swept across the region and turned day into night.

Many families lost their farms. Hundreds of thousands of people left the Plains, many heading west to California in search of farm work. In 1935, Congress created the Soil Conservation Service, which taught farmers to plant windbreaks of trees, rotate crops, and plow along the curves of the land to hold the soil.

stimuli.title: Document: The National Labor Relations Act (Wagner Act), 1935
stimuli.html:
Section 1 (excerpts)

The denial by employers of the right of employees to organize and the refusal by employers to accept the procedure of collective bargaining lead to strikes and other forms of industrial strife or unrest….

The inequality of bargaining power between employees who do not possess full freedom of association or actual liberty of contract, and employers who are organized in the corporate or other forms of ownership association substantially burdens and affects the flow of commerce, and tends to aggravate recurrent business depressions, by depressing wage rates and the purchasing power of wage earners in industry….

Experience has proved that protection by law of the right of employees to organize and bargain collectively safeguards commerce from injury, impairment, or interruption, and promotes the flow of commerce by removing certain recognized sources of industrial strife and unrest… and by restoring equality of bargaining power between employers and employees.

strife = conflict; aggravate = make worse; recurrent = repeated; commerce = trade and business
stimuli.source: Source: National Labor Relations Act, 49 Stat. 449 (1935), Section 1.

stimuli.title: Reading: The Pullman Strike of 1894
stimuli.html:
(1) In the 1880s, George Pullman, whose company built the famous Pullman sleeping cars used by railroads, built a company town just south of Chicago. Most of his workers lived in houses they rented from the company.

(2) When a severe economic depression began in 1893 and orders for new cars fell, the Pullman company cut workers' wages by 20 to 30 percent. It did not lower the rents in the company town. In May 1894, many Pullman workers walked off the job.

(3) Many of the strikers belonged to the American Railway Union (ARU), led by Eugene V. Debs. In late June, the ARU began a boycott in support of the Pullman workers: its members across the country refused to work on any train that included a Pullman car. At its peak, about 250,000 workers in 27 states took part, and rail traffic slowed or stopped across much of the nation.

(4) The railroads turned to the federal government. A federal court issued an injunction, a court order, forbidding the union's leaders from interfering with trains that carried the U.S. mail. In early July, President Grover Cleveland sent federal troops to Chicago, even though the governor of Illinois objected. Violence followed, and dozens of people were killed.

(5) The strike soon collapsed, and Debs was sentenced to six months in jail for disobeying the court order. Meanwhile, Congress had voted to make Labor Day a national holiday, and Cleveland signed that law on June 28, 1894, while the boycott was under way.

stimuli.title: Reading: The Tennessee Valley Authority
stimuli.html:
(1) In 1933, the valley of the Tennessee River, which covers parts of seven states, was one of the poorest regions in the United States. Floods along the river regularly destroyed crops and homes. Years of farming had worn out and eroded much of the soil, and many farm families had no electricity.

(2) On May 18, 1933, Congress created the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) as part of President Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal. The TVA built a series of dams on the Tennessee River and its branches. The dams held back floodwaters, deepened the river for barges, and used falling water to generate electricity.

(3) Low-cost electricity brought lights, radios, and electric pumps to many farms, and new factories opened in the region. The TVA also showed farmers how to use fertilizer and plant cover crops to rebuild worn-out soil.

(4) The changes had costs. The lakes that formed behind the dams flooded farmland, towns, and cemeteries. Thousands of families were required to sell their land and move away.

stimuli.title: Document: President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Message to Congress, May 24, 1937
stimuli.html:
Our Nation so richly endowed with natural resources and with a capable and industrious population should be able to devise ways and means of insuring to all our able-bodied working men and women a fair day's pay for a fair day's work. A self-supporting and self-respecting democracy can plead no justification for the existence of child labor, no economic reason for chiseling workers' wages or stretching workers' hours.

…All but the hopelessly reactionary will agree that to conserve our primary resources of man power, government must have some control over maximum hours, minimum wages, the evil of child labor and the exploitation of unorganized labor.

endowed = supplied; chiseling = cheating; reactionary = strongly opposed to change; exploitation = unfair use
stimuli.source: Source: Franklin D. Roosevelt, Message to Congress on Establishing Minimum Wages and Maximum Hours, May 24, 1937. Congress passed the Fair Labor Standards Act the next year.

items.skill: Cause and effect in economic history
items.prompt: According to the passage, why did many workers form labor unions?
options: Acting as a group gave them a better chance of winning higher pay and safer conditions.
The federal government required every factory worker in the country to join a union.
Factory owners asked their workers to organize so that their mills would produce more.
Unions helped factory workers leave their jobs and find better-paying work on farms.
why: The passage never says union membership was required. The 1935 law in paragraph 5 protected the right to form unions, which is different from requiring it.
Nothing in the passage says owners wanted unions. Paragraph 3 says workers organized to win better pay and conditions from employers.
The passage says unions bargained with employers for their members. It never connects unions to farm work.
items.hint: Paragraph 3 begins with the word "Because." Read that sentence closely.
items.explain:
Paragraph 3 says that "because one worker could easily be replaced, many workers decided that they had a better chance of winning higher pay and safer conditions if they acted together." That is the reason unions formed.

The choice about a government requirement is tempting because paragraph 5 mentions a federal law, but that law protected the right to form unions; it did not require anyone to join.

Fairview
Dunmore
Brightwater

Brightwater is at 2°N, 4°E. The latitude is right, but it is to the right of the prime meridian, which is east, not west.
items.hint: Latitude comes first. Go 2 lines up from the equator, then 4 lines left of the prime meridian.
items.explain:
Step 1: 2°N means 2 lines above the equator.
Step 2: 4°W means 4 lines left of the prime meridian.
Step 3: The town at that point is Port Alder.

Fairview (4°N, 2°W) is the most common wrong answer: it comes from reversing the numbers.

items.prompt: Drag each reason for migrating into the correct category.

A country offers free farmland to new settlers.
Relatives already living in the new country can help newcomers find housing.
A war breaks out in the family's home region.
items.why: The most common mistake is calling the relatives a push factor because family influenced the move. The relatives live in the new place and make it more attractive, so they are a pull factor.
items.hint: Ask: Is this a problem with the place people are leaving, or an attraction of the place they are going?
items.explain:
Push factors (problems in the old place): the drought, religious persecution, and the war.

Pull factors (attractions of the new place): higher-paying factory jobs, free farmland, and relatives who can help with housing.

items.prompt: A government begins charging importers a 20 percent tax on every foreign-made washing machine that enters the country. What kind of trade policy is this?
options: A tariff
A quota
An embargo
A free-trade agreement
why: A quota limits the number of goods that may be imported. This policy does not cap the number; it charges a tax on each one.
An embargo bans trade completely. Washing machines can still be imported here; they are just taxed.
A free-trade agreement lowers barriers between countries. A new tax on imports is a barrier, not the removal of one.
items.hint: Is the policy a tax, a limit on the amount, or a complete ban?
items.explain: A tax on imported goods is a tariff. A quota would limit the number of washing machines, an embargo would ban them, and a free-trade agreement would remove barriers instead of adding one.

items.prompt: Which statement is supported by the graph?

By the 1880 census, a majority of the people in the United States already lived in urban areas.
The largest ten-year increase in the urban share shown on the graph came between 1870 and 1880.
why: The line rises in every decade (19.8, 25.7, 28.2, 35.1, 39.6, 45.6, 51.2). It never falls.
In 1880 the urban share was only 28.2%, far less than half. A majority means more than 50%.
The 1870–1880 increase (28.2 − 25.7 = 2.5 points) was the smallest. The largest was 1880–1890 (35.1 − 28.2 = 6.9 points).
items.hint: Look for the first point on the line that is above 50%. Then check each ten-year change.
items.explain:
The values are 19.8, 25.7, 28.2, 35.1, 39.6, 45.6, and 51.2. Only 1920 (51.2%) is above 50%, so 1920 is the first year shown with an urban majority.

The line rises every decade, so it never fell. In 1880 only 28.2% lived in urban areas. The 1870–1880 increase (2.5 points) was the smallest, not the largest; the largest was 1880–1890 (6.9 points).
